title: He was raving all night about a black panther
html_source:
Haines, the English house guest, suffers from night terrors – having the night before raved after dreaming of a black panther. Later in the novel the black panther becomes for Bloom a symbol carrying overtones of divinity.

Likely an allusion to the three animals mentioned in the opening of Dante’s Divine Comedy. In the first canto (Canto I, 30-36) Dante the pilgrim is lost in a remote area when:

And lo! almost where the ascent began,
A panther light and swift exceedingly,
Which with a spotted skin was covered o'er!

And never moved she from before my face,
Nay, rather did impede so much my way,
That many times I to return had turned.

(Longfellow trans.)

Although Longfellow translates “panther”, the animal mentioned here, “una lonza” is actually a leopard; throughout the first Canto Dante also encounters a lion and a she-wolf. Respectively, they are thought to be symbols of lust, pride and avarice.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Many folk suggest Dante’s Panther is an allegory for Florence and worldly pleasures, and Dante’s anger at their failure to revolt. Given Haines is English is this an allegory for Ireland-England relations and the Irish Rising? He will shoot him if he doesn’t stop?
The ‘blacks’ are clarified below and the following note illustrates this sourced from
http://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Italian/DantnotesInf.htm#_Toc64100649

Salvation of Italy

There are various interpretations of Dante’s imagery, for example that the leopard (panther) represents Florence and worldly pleasure, lust or envy; the lion the Royal House of France, and ambition or pride; the she-wolf the Papacy, and avarice. Lust, pride and avarice are the three roots of sin. The imagery of the three animals may come from Jeremiah (v.6). The she-wolf, the Papacy, made many alliances.

The Greyhound (Veltro) has been suggested to be Can Grande della Scala, born in Verona, between Feltro in Venetia and Montefeltro in Romagna, the great Ghibelline leader. Dante’s later patron, he may have been regarded by Dante as the deliverer who would restore Imperial power, reinstitute Roman law, eliminate avarice, bring peace, and establish a reformed order of things.

Dante, whose father Aldighiero was a Guelf, and supporter of the papacy, traced his ancestry back to Cacciaguida, a crusader under Emperor Conrad III, and identified with the Romans who had allied Florence to Imperial Rome. He was of the populo vecchio, the populus, the old inhabitants, not the plebs, from Fiesole etc. Dante’s opposition however to the dishonesty and corruption of the Papacy under Boniface VIII aligned him with the Ghibelline pro-Imperial cause, and opposed him to the pro-Papacy Guelfs. The Florentine families also split between the local Bianchi (white) and Neri (black) factions. Dante’s family belonged to the Bianchi. Ultimately the Bianchi combined with the old half-suppressed Ghibelline party, and the Neri aligned with the Papacy, claiming to represent the old Guelph traditions of Florence.

Dante’s personal ideals when fully developed were for an apolitical Church, and an earthly Empire, both enfranchised by God, supreme in their own spheres, one of spiritual and the other temporal power. He was therefore opposed to the Guelf principles of his father (the Ultramontanism of Gregory VII and Innocent III), and to the democracy and plutocracy of Florence. He was equally opposed to the supremacy of State over Church asserted by the Emperors Henry IV and Frederick II, by Henry II of England, and Philip the Fair of France. Dante therefore found himself ‘a party of one’ caught in the cross-currents of his time, supporting an autocratic view of the Imperial State, and a desire for a reformed, spiritual Papacy.

An alternative candidate for ‘the Greyhound’ is Uguccione della Faggiuola, head of the Ghibelline forces at Lucca in 1315 when the Guelphs were driven out, and at the siege of Montecatini (within ten miles of Florence) where he gained a decisive victory. However Uguccione was eclipsed by 1316.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: This is generally accepted to have a biographical source: the real-life counterpart to Haines (Samuel Chenevix Trench) had a dream about a black panther in this very Martello tower, and in his distress fired a pistol at the wall.

Have any other Joyce commentators suggested this is a Dante allusion? It might well be, all this stuff is interesting, but it does kind of run away from Ulysses without really fleshing out the connection … It’s an annotation on Dante way more than it is anything else …

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I agree with jayclay about the discussion of Dante being irrelevant.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: @DavidDevalle Thanks for replying to this! I’d more or less forgotten I’d left this suggestion—and thanks for pointing me to Mary Reynolds. I’ve managed to read the p. 36 you specified, but (without having read the rest of her book, and admittedly not being myself very familiar with Dante; I’m sure I’ve got a partial view of the whole thing) the ‘panther’ referenced by that page is the phrase ‘black panther vampire’, which Stephen utters as a kind of epithet for Bloom in the ‘Circe’ episode. The reverberations and recurrences of the ‘black panther’ motif or symbol no doubt stem from its appearance in ‘Telemachus’, but I’m not convinced that the first appearance of the panther was even an allusion to Dante. Would Joyce or Stephen, both accomplished in Italian (Joyce had certainly read the Commedia in Italian before 1904), think of it as Dante’s panther instead of what it is in Italian: a leopard? Possibly, if Longfellow was what stuck in his mind, I suppose. When Reynolds mentions when, as you say, ‘Leopold recognises’ the Yeats poem which references Dante, she actually writes that Bloom ‘recogniz[es] a reference to poetry though he does not know whose’. And when she discusses the ‘black panther vampire’, the connection to Dante is not made via the ‘panther’ or ‘leopard’; she writes of this as ‘reflecting Dante’s plea for help against “the beast that turned me back.”’ This ‘beast’ isn’t the first of the animals Dante encounters (not a panther or a leopard)—it’s a she-wolf. I’m grateful to have been directed to the Reynolds, but as far as I can see she doesn’t claim that the panther in Telemachus is meant to reflect Dante’s ‘panther’; instead, she suggests that Stephen has panthers on the brain in such a way that later brings out references to Dante, which are tied to the opening of Canto 1 but not to the actual appearance in it of any panther.

I wasn’t trying to suggest that ‘Joyce didn’t know that about the panther’. (Didn’t know what? Its symbolic connection to Florence?) I was addressing the scope of this particular annotation. As I can see, it identifies an allusion to Dante (well and good), and suggests some significance of this panther (or leopard) to Dante, while making a connection between ‘the worldly pleasures of Florence’ and the English response to the Rising and as colonisers in general (well and good, and I feel a very valid point)—but then the rest of it just discusses Dante’s life and his relationship with the church and state, without trying to draw a parallel to Joyce. Maybe the parallels are supposed to be obvious, but I don’t really see them and I think many others won’t either.

So by ‘fleshing out the connection’, I meant: I wasn’t convinced that the discussion of Dante and nothing but Dante added a great deal to the annotation on this particular moment. This is too long for a genius annotation, and I think many would be confused as to how the Dante info relates to this specific description of Haines’s dream.

I’m aware that this was probably originally added as a suggestion, and I think it was a mistake to have integrated it without editing it. This annotation is now very choppy and not in line with how annotations here should be. The biographical info on Dante would have been fine as an illuminating comment below the annotation, but not as the bulk of it.

And I wasn’t claiming a biographical connection with ‘Introibo ad altare Dei’ but very specifically with Haines’s dream (I didn’t mention the parody of Catholic Mass at all): as I wrote,

the real-life counterpart to Haines (Samuel Chenevix Trench) had a dream about a black panther in this very Martello tower, and in his distress fired a pistol at the wall.

And I’m not sure what you meant by the following:

Mulligan murmuring “Introibo ad altare Dei” is no doubt biographical but that does not mean the first scene parody of the Catholic Mass and Joyce’s intent concerning Stephen’s sin about his mother is contextualised and interwoven with the Hellenic and Hebraic context of the journey evoking such as Thalatta.

Did you mean to write, ‘that does not mean the first scene parody […] isn’t contextualised and interwoven […]’? I would agree that the fact that something is biographical doesn’t mean it doesn’t have wider significance and complexity. I think biographical details are often minor points—they can help anchor us while we’re reading, but don’t often constitute an interpretation. My bringing up the point of a biographical parallel was to try to add an interesting (and documented) detail to this annotation, not to try to dismiss the more interesting suggestions surrounding allusions and symbolic significance.

Anyway, I hope we’re not talking at cross-purposes, and I hope what I’ve written is halfway intelligible. Forgive me if I seem to have addressed things that you didn’t write or don’t agree with—as I said above, the fact that this annotation is clogged up with unedited proposed suggestions is the main reason why it’s overlong and even confusing; and it would take some time to figure out which contributions belong to whom. I really do appreciate that you took the time to address what I wrote. :)
